**[central]** Background/distractor motion measurably delays detection of a feature change in a concurrently-monitored item: mean RT to detect a 30° orientation change was 439 ms (SD 58) in stationary displays vs 519 ms (SD 69) in moving displays — an ~80 ms cost with a very large effect size, F(1,27) = 97.52, p < 0.001, η²p = 0.783 (Exp. 1, N = 30, Gabor patches, set sizes 1–8, item speeds 85–254 px/s).

**[central]** Display density and motion interact multiplicatively rather than additively: RT rose with set size at a static search slope of 9.7 ms/item (2–8 items), F(6,162) = 23.24, p < 0.001, η²p = 0.463, and the motion penalty was LARGER at larger set sizes.

**[central]** In a controlled dual-task lab experiment (n=26, between-subjects, 3 min baseline + 12 min dual task, primary task = sorting 1500 e-mails), a small on-screen text strip (a Ticker occupying 3% of monitor height) produced significantly better recall of the displayed information than an abstract color-coded physical orb placed within 50° of focal vision: mean 3.2 vs 1.9 correct of 5 knowledge questions, t(24) = −2.19, p = 0.038 — while self-reported awareness was identical (2.9, σ=0.9) for both.

**[central]** Motion of the changing element itself is a SECOND, independent source of detection delay, additive to the surrounding-motion cost: in mixed displays (half static, half moving), detection of a change on a moving target was 43 ms slower than on a static target (623 ms vs 580 ms, p = 0.011); full ordering was pure-static 544 ms < mixed-static 580 ms < mixed-moving 623 ms < pure-moving 635 ms, F(3,84) = 25.53, p < 0.001, η²p = 0.477 (Exp. 2, N = 31).

**[central]** Operator expertise does not inoculate against inattentional blindness: 84 infantry personnel with 1–19 years and a mean of ~250 hours of real CCTV monitoring experience were statistically indistinguishable from 87 naive civilians, χ²(1, N=171)=0.11, p=.746, w=0.02 (near-zero effect).

**[central]** Physical HUD characteristics — a 40% increase in on-screen HUD area (9% vs 15% of screen, The Witcher III, N=40) and HUD main colour (red vs blue, CS:GO, N=36) — produced no significant effect on player performance or subjective experience, with effect sizes at or near zero (η²p < .01 in most tests).

**[central]** Reducing HUD content per se does not measurably help: removing game-control-mapping elements from the Zelda: Skyward Sword HUD (N=41) changed neither task progress (F(1,39)=1.11, p=.30, η²p=.03) nor immersion (F(1,39)=2.41, p=.13, η²p=.06), for experts or novices — a direct non-replication of the craft belief (and Iacovides et al. 2015's finding) that a minimal HUD improves expert immersion.

**[central]** Removing HUD elements that carry information necessary for the main task ('main' elements: avatar status, mini-map orientation) caused large, highly significant performance decrements in League of Legends (η²p = .41 and .67), whereas removing task-irrelevant 'secondary' elements (score, pseudonyms, item counts) left performance close to the full HUD — i.e. it is the task-value of an element, not the amount of chrome, that governs measured outcomes.

**[central]** Task-relevance of the unexpected stimulus is the dominant moderator of whether it is noticed: 79% missed it when it was task-irrelevant (a pirate in costume) versus 55% when task-relevant (a suspicious parcel), χ²(1, N=171)=10.53, p<.001, w=0.25 (small-to-moderate effect).

**[central]** The embellishment benefit is a long-term-memory effect, not a real-time reading effect: after a five-minute filled gap there was no recall advantage (subject t9=1.24 p=.124; categories t9=1.21 p=.129; trend t9=0.35 p=.369, n=10), while after 12–22 days every recall measure favored the embellished charts (subject t9=2.56 p=.015; categories t9=5.03 p≈.000; trend t9=1.95 p=.042; value message t9=2.41 p=.020, n=10).
